terms.gloss: foresee; provide for, take care in advance
terms.grammar: verb, second conjugation; with accusative, or dative (provide for), or nē
evidence: Cic. Fam. 9.18.4: āctum dē tē est, nisi prōvidēs (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Both halves of “anticipate”: to see what is coming (quae ēventūra sunt prōvidēre) and to see to it in time (reī frūmentāriae prōvidēre, to make sure of supplies).

terms.gloss: take beforehand, anticipate (a feeling, an event)
evidence: Cic. Att. 8.14: quī anticipēs ejus reī molestiam, quam trīduō scītūrus sīs (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: To take something up before its time: to fret over news before it comes (Cicero, below), to die before one’s time (mortem, Suet. Tib. 61). Not “expect” (see wait).

terms.gloss: take in advance; enjoy in advance
evidence: Cic. Phil. 13.45: praecipiō gaudia suppliciōrum vestrōrum (Antony, quoted; Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: To get a pleasure or an advantage ahead of time; its everyday sense is to instruct, so the context must make this one plain.

phrases.latin: āctum dē tē est, nisi prōvidēs
phrases.english: you’re done for unless you look ahead

phrases.latin: quī anticipēs ejus reī molestiam, quam trīduō scītūrus sīs
phrases.english: for you to suffer in advance over a matter you will know about in three days
